slides.title: Welcome to Fractions Kingdom!
bullets: Sharing sweet Georgia treats in Macon
slides.narration: Welcome, math explorer! Imagine you and a friend are sharing delicious Georgia peach pies. Maya has one third of a pie, and Leo has one fourth. How much pie do they have together? Let's find out!

slides.title: The Golden Rule: Like Denominators
bullets: Denominator tells the total equal slices in a whole
You CANNOT add slices of different sizes
Find a Common Denominator before adding
slides.narration: Here is the golden rule of fractions: the denominator tells us how many equal pieces make up the whole pie. If the bottom numbers are different, the slices are different sizes! We must cut them so they match.

slides.title: Finding Equivalent Fractions
slides.narration: Let's find a common multiple for 3 and 4. The least common denominator is 12! Multiplying top and bottom of one third by 4 gives 4 twelfths. Multiplying one fourth by 3 gives 3 twelfths. Now our slices match perfectly!

slides.title: Adding the Numerators
slides.narration: Step four is easy! Now that both fractions have 12 on the bottom, simply add the tops: 4 plus 3 equals 7. Keep the bottom 12. Together they drank 7 twelfths of a gallon!

slides.title: Beware the Denominator Trap!
bullets: Denominators describe slice size, not count
Always keep the common denominator identical
slides.narration: Watch out for the sneakiest trap in math! Never add the bottom denominators together. One third plus one fourth is NOT two sevenths! Always keep your common denominator identical.

slides.title: Ready for the Quest Arena!
bullets: Level up from Easy to Hard
slides.narration: Fantastic job! You now possess the power to defeat any fraction with unlike denominators. Step into the arena, solve your practice challenges, and claim your victory badge!

slides.title: Dividing Fractions: Appalachian Trail Adventure
bullets: Packing trail mix for a mountain hike
slides.narration: Welcome to Grade 6 Fraction Mastery! You are packing snacks for a hike on Georgia's Appalachian Trail. You have 3 fourths of a pound of trail mix, and each snack bag holds 1 eighth of a pound. How many bags can you fill?

slides.title: What Fraction Division Really Means
bullets: Visual fraction models show the groups
slides.narration: Dividing fractions simply asks: how many small groups fit inside the bigger amount? We want to see how many 1 eighth pieces fit into 3 fourths.

slides.title: The Magic Rule: Keep, Change, Flip!
slides.narration: Here is the secret weapon: Keep, Change, Flip! Keep the first fraction as 3 fourths. Change division to multiplication. And flip the second fraction upside-down into 8 over 1, its reciprocal!

slides.title: Multiply Across & Simplify
slides.narration: Now multiply straight across: 3 times 8 equals 24, and 4 times 1 equals 4. 24 divided by 4 equals 6 whole snack bags! You have enough fuel for the entire hike.

slides.title: Watch Out for the Flip Trap!
bullets: Always flip ONLY the second fraction (the divisor)
No common denominator needed for division!
slides.narration: Beware of the flip trap! Never flip the first fraction. Only flip the divisor on the right. And remember: you do not need common denominators when doing Keep-Change-Flip!

slides.title: Claim the Fraction Master Crown!
slides.narration: You are now officially a fraction division champion! Step into the arena, prove your skills, and let's conquer the leaderboard!

slides.title: Welcome to Decimals Domain!
bullets: Shopping at the Atlanta Farmer's Market
slides.narration: Welcome to Decimals Domain! We use decimals every single day, especially with money. Suppose you buy sweet Georgia Vidalia onions for 3 dollars and 45 cents, and fresh peaches for 2 dollars and 80 cents.

slides.title: The Golden Rule: Align the Decimal Points
bullets: Always line up the dots vertically!
slides.narration: The number one rule for adding and subtracting decimals is simple: line up the decimal points vertically! That guarantees tenths line up with tenths, and hundredths with hundredths.

slides.title: Add Like Whole Numbers
slides.narration: Add each column from right to left just like regular numbers. 5 plus 0 is 5. 4 plus 8 is 12 tenths, so write 2 and carry 1. 1 plus 3 plus 2 equals 6. Bring the decimal straight down: 6 dollars and 25 cents!

slides.title: Placeholder Zeros in Subtraction
bullets: Add trailing zeros so columns match
slides.narration: When subtracting decimals, always use placeholder zeros! In 4 point 5 0 minus 1 point 6 5, the zero in the hundredths place lets you borrow and subtract accurately to get 2 point 8 5.

slides.title: Beware the Right-Align Trap!
bullets: 🚫 TRAP: Lining numbers up on the right edge
Never treat decimals as whole numbers without dots
The decimal point controls the place value!
slides.narration: Watch out for the right-align trap! Don't line numbers up on the right edge. If you don't align the dots, you will add tenths to hundredths and your answer will be way off!

slides.title: You're Ready for Decimals Quest!
slides.narration: You are ready to roll! Keep your dots aligned, trust your math, and jump into the practice round to earn maximum XP!

slides.title: Welcome to Ratios Realm!
bullets: Ratio: 3 cups lemon juice to 2 cups sugar
slides.narration: Welcome to Ratios Realm! A ratio compares two quantities. Picture mixing sweet Georgia lemonade: for every 3 cups of fresh lemon juice, you need 2 cups of sugar. That's a 3 to 2 ratio!

slides.title: Understanding Multiplicative Comparisons
bullets: Ratios grow by MULTIPLYING, not adding
Part-to-whole: lemon juice to total punch
slides.narration: Ratios grow through multiplication! If you make a bigger pitcher, you scale up both ingredients by multiplying by the exact same number.

slides.title: Scaling Equivalent Ratios
bullets: Original: 3 cups lemon to 2 cups sugar
slides.narration: Let's make a party batch! If we triple the recipe, multiply both sides by 3: 3 times 3 gives 9 cups of lemon juice, and 2 times 3 gives 6 cups of sugar. The flavor stays perfectly balanced!

slides.title: Unit Rates: Price per Single Item
bullets: Unit Rate formula: Total Cost ÷ Quantity
slides.narration: A unit rate tells you how much for ONE single item. At a Macon peach stand, 4 peaches cost 6 dollars. Divide 6 by 4 to discover each peach costs 1 dollar and 50 cents!

slides.title: Trap Alert: Never Scale by Adding!
bullets: 🚫 TRAP: Adding the same number to both terms
3:2 + 1 to each does NOT make an equivalent ratio
Always multiply or divide by the scale factor!
slides.narration: Be on alert! Never scale a ratio by adding. If you add 1 to each term, turning 3 to 2 into 4 to 3, the recipe loses its sweet flavor! Always multiply or divide.

slides.title: Unleash Your Ratio Power!
slides.narration: You have mastered ratio tables and unit rates! Now head into the arena and show your proportional thinking power!

slides.title: Welcome to Geometry Citadel!
slides.narration: Welcome to Geometry Citadel! Geometry helps us build real things. Imagine planning a community garden in Savannah: you need fencing for the outside perimeter, and fertile soil for the area inside!

slides.title: Perimeter vs Area: Fence vs Floor
bullets: Perimeter (P): distance all the way AROUND
slides.narration: Remember the difference: Perimeter is the fence around the edge, measured in linear feet. Area is the carpet covering the inside floor, measured in square feet!

slides.title: Rectangle Calculations
bullets: Garden plot: Length = 8 ft, Width = 5 ft
slides.narration: For our garden measuring 8 by 5 feet, the perimeter is 2 times 13, which is 26 feet of fence. The area is 8 times 5, which equals 40 square feet of planting soil!

slides.title: Triangle Area: Half a Rectangle!
bullets: Every triangle is exactly HALF of a rectangle
Sail on Lake Lanier: Base = 8m, Height = 5m
slides.narration: Here is a mind-blowing secret: every triangle is exactly half of a rectangle! That's why the formula is base times height divided by 2. An 8 by 5 meter sail has an area of 40 divided by 2, which is 20 square meters!

slides.title: Trap Alert: Don't Forget to Divide by 2!
bullets: 🚫 TRAP: Forgetting to divide by 2 for triangles
Base times height gives the whole rectangle
Always take half for the triangle!
slides.narration: Avoid the number one geometry mistake: never forget to divide by 2 when finding triangle area! Base times height gives the whole box—you must cut it in half for the triangle.

slides.title: Conquer the Citadel!
slides.narration: You are equipped with the architect's toolkit! Step into the practice arena, solve your challenges, and conquer Geometry Citadel!
